stands.title: Navarre picks the valley
stands.situation: Autumn 1953. Navarre has evacuated Na San and plans to stay on the defensive in the north while Operation Atlante clears Interzone V. The Deuxième Bureau says Giáp's reserve divisions may move toward Lai Châu and Laos. Lai Châu, capital of the French-allied Tai Federation, is indefensible in a gorge under the mountains. Điện Biên Phủ, 113 km south, has the only other 'Dakotable' airfield in the northwest, the region's best rice land, and sits on the route to Luang Prabang.

options.text: Evacuate Lai Châu and give up the Tai country.

stands.decided: Operation Castor (parachute seizure of Điện Biên Phủ) and Operation Pollux (evacuation of Lai Châu), launched 20 November 1953.
stands.why: To parry another invasion of upper Laos, which Navarre felt bound to defend, keep the Tai and GMI guerrillas in the war, and project mobile columns across northwest Tonkin from an all-weather airfield.
stands.outcome: Castor succeeded, but the Tai columns from Lai Châu were cut to pieces by 13 December, and within four weeks sorties beyond the valley had become very risky. Navarre's and Cogny's differing ideas of the base's purpose persisted.
questions: Navarre and Cogny agreed on the place but not the purpose. What did that gap cost the garrison in the next three months?
Which of Navarre's reasons depended on the base being an offensive hub, and which still held once it was encircled?
What intelligence would have told Navarre that the valley floor could be dominated from the surrounding ridges?

stands.title: Giáp's hardest decision
stands.placeName: Eastern heights (ridges east of the Five Hills)
stands.situation: Morning of 26 January. A three-day assault ordered at the Tham Púa briefing on 14 January is due at 17:00, already postponed once because its timing may have leaked. Guns sit in exposed positions; only about 2,000 105mm shells are allotted. The French have added battalions, wire and the 'Wavebreaker' in front of the 308th Division's planned axis. Giáp's staff, division commanders and Chinese advisers favour attacking now, before the camp grows stronger and supply lines lengthen into the rains.

options.text: Attack as planned: 'swift attack, swift victory', a simultaneous thrust from the west into de Castries' HQ with the eastern hills taken by the 312th and 316th.

stands.decided: Call off the attack hours before H-hour, pull troops and guns back, and prepare a 'steady attack, steady advance' siege; send the 308th Division toward Luang Prabang as a diversion.
stands.why: Giáp judged the camp no longer a temporary defence. His army had never destroyed more than one reinforced fortified battalion, had no experience coordinating infantry with heavy guns, and would have to fight by day across open fields against air and armour. No one at the meeting would guarantee success.
stands.outcome: The guns were hauled out and re-emplaced in concealed casemates by March; logistics requirements roughly tripled. Boylan & Olivier judge that the planned January assault would have been a French victory.
questions: What made Giáp confident enough to overrule his staff and advisers, and what did he risk politically by doing so?
How would the battle have gone if the French had read the 26 January pull-back correctly?
Compare the information Giáp had about the French with what Navarre had about Giáp's artillery.

stands.title: Reinforce before the storm? Piroth's assurances
stands.maker: Gen. Navarre, with Gen. Cogny and Col. de Castries
stands.situation: Early March. The VPA has not attacked. Its guns are in place and stocked, yet the French have found only a handful and destroyed none of the casemates; GONO's own guns sit in open pits under observation from the ridges. Piroth tells visitors the enemy cannot bring guns in, will be smashed if he does, and cannot keep them supplied, but privately admits the situation 'may be irreversible'. On a visit on 4 March, Navarre is uneasy about the unseen artillery.

stands.decided: No reinforcement before the battle; GONO's leadership stays confident it will inflict a severe defeat and does not want to deter the attack.
stands.why: Cogny opposed sending more battalions; de Castries judged that extra battalions could not be supplied, and that strongpoints for them could not be built for lack of engineering materials. Faith that artillery and air power would silence the VPA guns did the rest.
stands.outcome: On 13 March the hidden batteries opened fire; Béatrice fell that night and Gabrielle the next. Piroth killed himself on 15 March.
questions: Piroth kept his doubts private to protect morale. What obligation does a staff officer have when he loses confidence in the plan?
Which of Piroth's three assumptions failed first, and could the garrison have tested it before 13 March?
Would two or three more battalions in early March have changed the outcome, or only Giáp's timing?

stands.title: 13 March: why Béatrice first?
stands.situation: Afternoon of 13 March. The siege plan is ready: three outer resistance centres (Him Lam, Độc Lập, Bản Kéo) form a screen north, north-east and north-west of the central sub-sector. Béatrice, held by III/13e DBLE, sits 2 km from Mường Thanh on the Tuần Giáo road, overlooked and isolated from help. The troops have been primed for victory by their commissars; a failed first battle would hurt morale badly.

options.text: The January concept: a main thrust from the west into the HQ with simultaneous attacks from several directions.

stands.decided: Open the campaign at 17:00 with a massed bombardment of the whole camp and an assault on Béatrice by the 141st and 209th Regiments, followed by Gabrielle the next night.
stands.why: Under 'strike surely' the first battle had to be a certain win: infantry three times stronger than the defenders, mortars and light artillery many times stronger, heavy guns tasked to protect the infantry and suppress French batteries.

stands.title: Gabrielle: counterattack or write it off?
stands.maker: Lt-Col. Pierre Langlais, under Col. de Castries
stands.situation: Before dawn on 15 March. Gabrielle, 4 km north and held by V/7e RTA, has fought all night; at 04:30 a shell kills or wounds its leaders and cuts it off from the artillery. Two VPA regiments are on the hill. Langlais has run the Main Position and reserves since 13 March; on 14 March two companies each of 1er BEP and 8e BPC were tied to the Central Subsector, so no full-strength battalion is free. Dawn will expose any column to VPA observers.

stands.decided: A two-company counterattack with all seven tanks set out at 05:15; at about 07:00 Langlais changed its mission to rescuing survivors. The garrison, thinking it was being evacuated, left the hill at 07:45-08:00.
stands.why: Langlais and de Castries had abandoned automatic counterattacks by dawn on 14 March and feared feints against the Main Position; Langlais, Boylan & Olivier argue, was already husbanding reserves.
stands.outcome: Gabrielle was lost. De Castries later told the Catroux Commission he had decided to shrink the defence to the central perimeter and Isabelle, with no attempt to retake Béatrice, Gabrielle or Anne-Marie, and that higher command approved.
questions: Does mission-type orders work when the mission itself ('retake, or at least recover survivors') contains two different end states?
What does the 05:15-08:00 timeline say about the effect of contradictory orders on a unit already in crisis?
Was writing off the north a sound economy of force or the moment GONO lost the initiative for good?

stands.decided: Halt the Éliane 2 assault and turn west against Huguette 6 (Huguette 7 had already fallen on 1-2 April) and the airstrip, using trenches; 10 April orders set saps toward Claudine 5 and Huguette 1, 4 and 5.

stands.why: Washington would not intervene; Dulles told Bidault B-29 intervention seemed out of the question. Cogny believed the exhausted defenders could not make a fighting withdrawal; by 7 May the Main Position could not hold until dark.

stands.title: 7 May: attack now, in daylight?
stands.situation: Midday on 7 May. Overnight, A1 fell after the mine and Éliane 4 and 10 went by morning, but the attack on Éliane 12 failed and Giáp is cautious. The French hold a pocket 700-1,000 m wide; reports of documents being burned suggest a breakout attempt that night. Ammunition aircraft turn back without dropping, explosions suggest weapons being destroyed, and French troops are seen throwing arms into the river.

stands.decided: At 15:00, after position 507 by the bridge went, order a general attack on the camp at once, in daylight, from east and west toward the command post.
stands.why: The garrison showed every sign of collapse, and waiting risked letting part of it slip out to Laos.
stands.outcome: White flags appeared; GONO declared a cease-fire for 17:30 and the command post was occupied. Isabelle's breakout that night was largely stopped by the 57th Regiment.

diplomacy.text: Berlin Conference of Foreign Ministers ends; communiqué agrees that a conference on Korea will meet at Geneva on 26 April and that 'the problem of restoring peace in Indochina will also be discussed'.
diplomacy.why: Fixed a negotiating deadline while the siege was being prepared: both sides now had reason to seek a battlefield result before Geneva, and the PRC was invited to the table.

diplomacy.text: Viet Minh assault opens on Béatrice (Him Lam); US Embassy Saigon reports approximately twenty 105s and some thirty 75s brought up, per French intelligence.
diplomacy.why: The diplomatic clock starts in earnest: the battle opens six weeks before Geneva, and US reporting already records Viet Minh artillery in quantity.

diplomacy.text: Radford polls the Joint Chiefs on offering US naval/air intervention at Dien Bien Phu. On 31 March all four service chiefs say no (Twining and Shepherd: not unless China intervenes). Asked a follow-up question on 2 April, Twining gives a 'qualified Yes' subject to French assurances; Ridgway, Carney and Shepherd stay opposed.
diplomacy.why: Only the Chairman favoured intervention; the service chiefs' memos are the documentary core of the Vulture debate.

diplomacy.text: British refusal. Eden returns to London; the Cabinet meets on Sunday 25 April with the Chiefs of Staff. That night in Geneva Eden tells Dulles the Chiefs are 'certain that air intervention at Dien Bien Phu would have no decisive effect'. On 27 April Churchill tells the Commons HMG gives no undertakings on military action 'in advance of the results of Geneva'.
diplomacy.why: Removed the allied cover Congress had demanded on 3 April; without Britain, 'united action' could not be assembled before the garrison fell.

contested.claim: Before the battle Piroth assured superiors that no Viet Minh gun would fire more than three rounds before French counter-battery fire destroyed it (wording varies by source).
contested.why: Widely repeated in secondary works (e.g. Fall 1966; Roy 1963; Windrow 2004) but always reported second-hand from officers' recollections or post-battle testimony; the exact words and occasion differ between versions. No contemporaneous document was located.

contested.claim: Last words before his suicide on the night of 14–15 March 1954, often given as 'Je suis complètement déshonoré' or a similar line.
contested.why: No one witnessed the suicide; versions come from later accounts. Grauwin, the garrison surgeon, says he learned of it second-hand from soldiers outside his dugout ('il s'est suicidé avec une grenade'). The death was also kept quiet at the time.

contested.who: René Cogny to Christian de Castries (radio, 7 May 1954)
contested.claim: Final radio exchange in which Cogny tells de Castries to cease fighting but without a white flag ('pas de drapeau blanc').
contested.why: A transcript is published in several French and English works and was reportedly recorded, but this compilation could not check a primary transcript or the cited recording. Wording differs between published versions.

contested.claim: Bidault later said Dulles offered France two atomic bombs for use at Dien Bien Phu, around 23–24 April 1954 in Paris.
contested.why: Rests on Bidault's later recollection, recounted in later works and on film; Dulles and US officials denied it. The FRUS record of the Paris talks (docs. 777, 778, 789) contains no such offer. It does show that a JCS study committee estimated 'three tactical A-weapons' could break the siege (FRUS XIII doc. 711).

contested.claim: Radford gave Ely a personal assurance in March 1954 that he would do his best to obtain US naval air support if Dien Bien Phu needed it.
contested.why: Cited by the French Cabinet on 4 April (Dillon tel. 3710) and in Ely's memoirs (pp. 76–77, 82–83). The FRUS editors state: 'U.S. records of the meetings… contain no reference to such an undertaking by Admiral Radford.'

contested.claim: Vulture was a JCS plan 'for using three small tactical atomic bombs'.
contested.why: Nixon's memoir (RN, 1978, p. 150, quoted in FRUS) runs together the conventional French 'Vautour' request and a separate JCS study of atomic use. On 24 April Radford told Ely he had never heard the name 'Operation Vulture' (FRUS XIII doc. 792).

contested.claim: Ho explained the battle by turning a hat upside down: the French in the bottom, the Viet Minh on the rim.
contested.why: A single-source anecdote from a sympathetic journalist, often repeated online with varying wording and date.

contested.claim: Calling the 26 January 1954 postponement 'the most difficult decision of my career' (wording varies).
contested.why: Common in online retellings and interviews; the 1964 FLPH text consulted here (pp. 90–92) explains the change of principle but does not use this phrase. Later memoirs (e.g. Điện Biên Phủ: Điểm hẹn lịch sử, 2000) may contain it but were not checked.

contested.who: René Cogny (per his staff, via journalists, to Consul Sturm)
contested.claim: Cogny 'never approved concept of Dien-Bien-Phu but accepted it as “a sporting proposition”', and remarked that it 'had changed color in his hands'.
contested.why: The FRUS telegram is genuine, but the words reach it through several hands (Cogny's cabinet chiefs and the journalist Robert Guillain, then Sturm) while Cogny and Navarre were already arguing over blame.

theory.cite: Fearon, James D. "Rationalist Explanations for War." International Organization 49, no. 3 (1995): 379-414.
theory.claim: Rational states that would prefer a negotiated settlement can still fight because each holds private information about its capabilities and resolve and has incentives to misrepresent it, alongside commitment problems and issue indivisibility.
theory.app: The size, placement and supply of the Viet Minh artillery was private information that Giap had every incentive to hide; the French committed to the valley on a belief about enemy capability that only battle could correct.

theory.cite: Slantchev, Branislav L. "Feigning Weakness." International Organization 64, no. 3 (2010): 357-388.
theory.claim: Revealing military strength can deter but also forfeits the advantage of surprise, so a state may rationally conceal its strength and appear weaker than it is, accepting a higher risk of war in exchange for better wartime prospects.
theory.app: By hiding its guns rather than displaying them, the Viet Minh let the French believe the garrison could hold, inviting the very battle in which concealed artillery would be decisive.

theory.cite: Green, Brendan Rittenhouse, and Austin Long. "Conceal or Reveal? Managing Clandestine Military Capabilities in Peacetime Competition." International Security 44, no. 3 (2020): 48-83.
theory.claim: States holding clandestine military capabilities face a trade-off: revealing them can shape an adversary's beliefs and behavior, but disclosure lets the adversary develop countermeasures and erodes the capability's wartime value.
theory.app: The casemated forward-slope guns were a capability whose value depended on staying hidden until 13 March; once unveiled they could no longer be pre-empted by counter-battery planning the French had not built for them.

theory.cite: Gartzke, Erik, and Jon R. Lindsay. "Weaving Tangled Webs: Offense, Defense, and Deception in Cyberspace." Security Studies 24, no. 2 (2015): 316-348.
theory.claim: Deception, not offense per se, is the defining logic of cyber operations, and deception is available to defenders as well as attackers, so the offense-defense balance depends on who can better exploit an adversary's reliance on information.
theory.app: Though written about cyberspace, the logic carries over: Viet Minh camouflage and night movement exploited French dependence on aerial reconnaissance, turning the French sensing advantage into a source of false confidence.

theory.cite: Betts, Richard K. "Analysis, War, and Decision: Why Intelligence Failures Are Inevitable." World Politics 31, no. 1 (1978): 61-89.
theory.claim: Major intelligence failures usually stem less from missing collection than from analysts' and decision makers' interpretation and use of information, and organizational reforms can reduce but not eliminate them.
theory.app: French commanders had warning indicators of Viet Minh build-up but read them through prior assumptions about what a guerrilla army could haul into the hills, a failure of analysis and decision rather than of collection alone.

theory.cite: Murphy, William T. "The French Defeat at Dien Bien Phu and the Limitation of Military Intelligence." International Journal of Intelligence and CounterIntelligence 39, no. 2 (2026): 486-518. First published online May 9, 2025.
theory.claim: French intelligence gathered substantial signals intelligence from decrypted Viet Minh radio traffic, while human and imagery intelligence were less effective; despite ample raw intelligence, French analysis and forecasting failed, and the article argues French passivity amounted to self-entrapment rather than a Viet Minh trap.
theory.app: This is the most direct scholarly treatment of the stand's intelligence question: the French were not blind, but their analysis of what the intercepts meant for artillery and logistics in the hills failed during nearly four months of inaction.

theory.cite: Fall, Bernard B. Hell in a Very Small Place: The Siege of Dien Bien Phu. Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott, 1967.
theory.claim: The standard English-language history of the siege, reconstructing French planning, the Viet Minh build-up and the battle in detail.
theory.app: Fall's narrative supplies the operational record for the staff ride: the French decision to fight in the valley, the reliance on counter-battery fire against guns that could not be located, and Piroth's suicide after the opening bombardment.

cf.lever: Operation Vulture/Vautour approved: US air intervention at Dien Bien Phu in April 1954
cf.change: What was actually proposed varied. On 4 April France asked for US carrier aircraft (FRUS XIII doc. 691). On 6 April it asked for 10–20 B-29s with US maintenance, possibly based in the Philippines (doc. 702). By 23 April Navarre's alternative was 'Operation Vautour… massive B-29 bombing' from US bases outside Indochina (doc. 778), and Ely spoke of '200 to 300 carrier aircraft' (doc. 777). A JCS study committee separately estimated that 'three tactical A-weapons' could break the siege (doc. 711). Secondary works put the B-29 force at 60 to 98 aircraft; those figures were not verified against a primary operational plan, and no Vulture operations order is printed in FRUS. On 24 April Radford said he had not heard the name (doc. 792). Sortie counts: none verified.

judgments.who: Adm. Arthur Radford, CJCS (3 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: Too late to save the garrison by airpower, but had airpower been committed three weeks earlier he felt 'reasonably certain' the Viet Minh would have been defeated.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 686 (Dulles memo for the file on 3 Apr congressional meeting), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d686

judgments.who: Gen. Matthew Ridgway, Army Chief of Staff (2 and 6 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: An 'emphatic' no. US capability for effective intervention was 'altogether disproportionate to the liability it would incur', the outcome at Dien Bien Phu would not decisively affect the military situation, and intervention would greatly raise the risk of general war. On 6 April he called it a 'dangerous strategic diversion' into a non-decisive theatre.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 682 (Ridgway memo, 2 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d682; FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 710 (Ridgway to JCS, 6 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d710

judgments.who: Adm. Robert Carney, CNO (2 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: Air intervention 'would improve the French tactical situation' at Dien Bien Phu, but the JCS were 'not prepared to state that such contribution would be decisive'.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 683 (Carney memo, 2 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d683

judgments.who: Gen. Nathan Twining, USAF Chief of Staff (31 Mar and 2 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: Radford's 31 March tally records 'not unless Chinese intervene'. Two days later Twining gave a 'qualified Yes', conditional on French acceptance of US command of air and naval elements, US training leadership, and real sovereignty for the Associated States.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 666 (JCS to SecDef, 31 Mar, with Radford's handwritten note), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d666; FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 684 (Twining to Radford, 2 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d684

judgments.who: Gen. Lemuel Shepherd, USMC Commandant (2 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: An 'unprofitable adventure'. The Viet Minh offered no target 'which our air will find remunerative', so the effect would fade and lead either to admitted failure or to ground intervention.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 685 (Shepherd memo, 2 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d685

judgments.who: French Chief of Air Staff (via Bidault, 4 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: US air intervention could provoke Chinese Communist air attacks on the Delta airfields.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 691 (Dillon tel. 3710), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d691

judgments.who: Gen. Paul Ely (22 and 24 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: On 22 April, 200–300 US carrier aircraft could still save the garrison, but 'hours were of the utmost importance' (as relayed by Laniel). By 24 April he accepted that intervention 'could have no direct bearing' on the battle and wanted it for its psychological effect before the fall.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 777 (MacArthur–Laniel, 23 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d777; FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 792 (Radford memo for file, 24 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d792

judgments.who: British Chiefs of Staff (via Eden, 25 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: 'certain that air intervention at Dien Bien Phu would have no decisive effect on that battle', and that undertaking it would be a mistake because no one could foresee where it would lead.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XVI, doc. 343 (Dulles–Eden memcon, 25 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v16/d343

judgments.who: John Foster Dulles (25 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: 'It is not certain, and probably unlikely, that intervention would in fact save Dien Bien Phu'. He judged it would strain relations with the UK, Australia and New Zealand and risk the US taking over the French ground role.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 798 (Dulte 3, 25 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d798

judgments.who: Dwight D. Eisenhower (26 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: Even if a 'sudden stroke' could save the garrison, on French terms 'the free world would lose more than it would gain'.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 2, doc. 808 (Eisenhower to Gruenther, 26 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p2/d808

judgments.who: George C. Herring and Richard H. Immerman (historians, 1984)
judgments.j: Revisit the 'day we didn't go to war' account, which blamed congressional reluctance. Their argument, summarised here from memory without checking against the text, is that the administration's own conditions (allies, French concessions, congressional backing) shaped the outcome. Verify before display.
judgments.src: George C. Herring and Richard H. Immerman, "Eisenhower, Dulles, and Dienbienphu: 'The Day We Didn't Go to War' Revisited," Journal of American History 71, no. 2 (1984): 343–63, https://doi.org/10.2307/1901759 (bibliographic data verified via OpenAlex; argument summary unverified)

cf.conf: high for the documented US and UK judgments; low for force-size figures (60–98 B-29s) and sortie numbers, which no primary source here confirms

cf.lever: The airstrip held longer: aircraft keep landing at the main strip, and at Isabelle's, beyond mid-March
cf.change: Evacuation of wounded, reinforcement by landing rather than parachute, and tonnage delivered. On 16 March the US Ambassador reported both airstrips 'unusable' under Viet Minh artillery, with the garrison relying 'entirely on airdrop'. Giáp names neutralising and then occupying the central airfield as an explicit second-phase aim (from 30 March). The date of the last landing (late March) comes from secondary literature and is not verified here.

judgments.who: US Embassy Saigon (Heath, 16 Mar 1954)
judgments.j: With the strips lost, the defence was 'heavily dependent upon airdrops from our loaned C–119s', and ground fog stopped counter-battery fire and air strikes on the guns. On this account the airstrip fell as a result of the artillery problem rather than as a separate failure.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 612 (Heath tel. 1697), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d612

judgments.who: Joseph Alsop (journalist), as reported by Philip Bonsal (22 Jan 1954)
judgments.j: Before the siege he predicted Dien Bien Phu would be 'a hopeless trap because the enemy will be able to cut off the French air lift'.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 519 (Bonsal to Heath, 22 Jan), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d519

judgments.who: Henri Navarre (as reported by Heath, 31 Dec 1953)
judgments.j: Chinese-supplied 37 mm anti-aircraft guns made the air role 'all-important and very difficult' and could stop French aircraft from silencing 105s placed on the heights.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 491 (Heath tel. 1151), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d491

judgments.who: Võ Nguyên Giáp (1964)
judgments.j: The central airfield, 'whose safety was badly needed to land reinforcements, food and ammunition', was brought under artillery fire in the first phase. Cutting it was a deliberate step in strangling supply, which he treats as decisive.
judgments.src: Võ Nguyên Giáp, Dien Bien Phu, 3rd ed. (Hanoi: FLPH, 1964), https://archive.org/details/dien-bien-phu-vo-nguyen-giap, pp. 115, 119–125 (airfield passages; pages for the second phase approximate)

judgments.who: US Consul Hanoi (Sturm), reporting Cogny's farewell remarks (16 Apr 1954)
judgments.j: 'A satisfactory air force establishment could radically change present relative positions at Dien-Bien-Phu.' It is not clear from the telegram whether this sentence is Cogny's view or Sturm's.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 751 (Sturm to State, 16 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d751

cf.conf: medium. Primary sources agree the airstrip was lost to artillery within days of 13 March, so this lever largely restates the artillery-concealment problem. No source quantifies how much difference a longer-held strip would have made.

cf.lever: Operation Albatros (breakout or sortie toward Laos) attempted earlier, in April rather than at the end
cf.change: Whether part of the garrison could have escaped south toward the Laos border and a relief force from Muong Sai (Condor), instead of being captured whole.

judgments.who: Gen. Paul Ely (22 Apr 1954, as relayed by Laniel)
judgments.j: Under existing circumstances (Ely replied) it 'could not make a fighting withdrawal'. A relief column of a few battalions from Laos 'might be feasible with US air intervention. Otherwise, it was not possible.'
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 777 (MacArthur–Laniel, 23 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d777

judgments.who: Henri Navarre (21–23 Apr 1954, as reported by Dejean)
judgments.j: A relief column from Muong Sai was 'not feasible because of lack of air power'; at most nine battalions could be found. He faced a choice between dropping his last reserves into the camp and keeping them for a relief column to cover a rearguard retreat.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 768 (McClintock tel. 2078, 22 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d768; FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 782 (McClintock tel. 2096, 23 Apr), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d782

judgments.who: Võ Nguyên Giáp (1964)
judgments.j: Says the VPA detected the French 'scheming to regroup his forces in three columns' to break out in early May, and tightened the encirclement to prevent it. In his account a breakout was foreseen and covered.
judgments.src: Võ Nguyên Giáp, Dien Bien Phu, 3rd ed. (Hanoi: FLPH, 1964), https://archive.org/details/dien-bien-phu-vo-nguyen-giap, p. 133

judgments.who: Secondary literature (e.g. Fall 1966; Windrow 2004)
judgments.j: Discusses Albatros and the late, partial breakout from Isabelle on 7–8 May. Specific judgments and pages were not verified here.
judgments.src: Bernard B. Fall, Hell in a Very Small Place (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1966/67); Martin Windrow, The Last Valley (London: Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 2004) – unverified

cf.conf: medium-low. The contemporaneous French judgments are documented (all pessimistic). Historians' views were not checked here.

cf.lever: Giáp keeps the January 'fight fast, win fast' plan (attack in late January instead of postponing and rebuilding for 13 March)
cf.change: An assault before the camp was fully fortified and before the artillery was re-emplaced in casemates. It would probably have come without the step-by-step siege, and before the Berlin Conference fixed the Geneva date (18 Feb).

judgments.who: Võ Nguyên Giáp (1964)
judgments.j: A rapid attack had advantages: fresh troops and an easier supply problem. But the troops 'lacked concrete experience in attacking fortified entrenched camps', and the enemy had reinforced, so 'a rapid attack to win a rapid victory would not vouch for complete success'. He switched to 'strike surely and advance cautiously'. The guns were hauled back out of their first positions and re-emplaced along new, camouflaged roads.
judgments.src: Võ Nguyên Giáp, Dien Bien Phu, 3rd ed. (Hanoi: FLPH, 1964), https://archive.org/details/dien-bien-phu-vo-nguyen-giap, pp. 90–92, 101

judgments.who: René Cogny (14 Jan 1954, as reported by Sturm)
judgments.j: The French expected the attack in mid-January and had confirmed divisions 308 and 316 around the camp: the defenders were waiting for it.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 506 (Sturm tel. 389, 15 Jan), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d506

judgments.who: Henri Navarre (as reported by Radford, 8 Jan 1954)
judgments.j: The Viet Minh 'might well be able to take Dien Bien Phu if they were willing to commit the three full divisions and take the resulting heavy losses'.
judgments.src: FRUS 1952–1954, vol. XIII pt. 1, doc. 499 (State–JCS/NSC record, 8 Jan 1954), https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v13p1/d499

judgments.who: Chen Jian (1993); Qiang Zhai (1992, 2000)
judgments.j: Using Chinese sources, these historians document the role of Chinese military advisers (headed by Wei Guoqing) in planning the campaign. How far the advisers shaped the January postponement is a question for those texts; their specific judgments and pages were not checked here.

viewsheds.method: Line of sight computed by Claude from Copernicus GLO-30 elevation data (radial ray casting, eye 3 m above ground for French posts and 2 m for Viet Minh points, target 2 m, 12 km radius, earth curvature and refraction). Today's town is filtered out of the valley floor; 1954 trenches, vegetation and camouflage are not modelled. Positions marked map-derived are uncertain by about 150 m.

findings: From a ridge point on the first heights east of the camp (609 m, about 2.8 km east of Éliane 2), 29 of the 37 mapped French positions, including the command post and Isabelle, are in direct line of sight. The ridge point is chosen for orientation; it is not a documented battery site.

The reverse also holds: 7 of the 7 French posts tested could see that ridge point. The ground itself did not hide those slopes. Giáp's own account says sham gun positions were built beside the real ones to draw and waste French fire (see Stand 2).

The preserved H6 rocket site sits in a fold: only 3.9 km² of ground is in view from it, and none of the French posts tested could see it. Rocket launchers fire indirectly, so they did not need to see their targets.
